chunks: "I'd start from the quantity I want, then ask what each sensor can and cannot tell me. First example: a wrist heart-rate sensor.
The optical signal, photoplethysmography, has the pulse but also motion artefacts that overlap in frequency when you run.
An accelerometer on the same board measures the motion but not the pulse.
I use the accelerometer as a noise reference in an adaptive filter, or in spectral subtraction, to remove the motion component from the optical signal and recover the heart rate.
Second: a phone deciding whether it is in your pocket.
Ambient light says dark, proximity says something is close, the accelerometer says the orientation is upright and moving as you walk.
Any one of them is ambiguous; together they are decisive, so the screen stays off. Third: a drone holding position indoors.
An optical-flow camera measures how fast the floor texture moves in the image, which is velocity divided by height plus rotation.
A rangefinder gives the height and a gyro gives the rotation to subtract, so velocity equals flow minus gyro rate, times height. With 2 metres height and 0.
5 radians per second of flow, with 0. 1 from rotation, that is 0. 8 metres per second.
Fourth: cameras and LiDAR with an IMU: the IMU bridges the gap between frames, removes motion distortion from a spinning LiDAR sweep, and the optical sensors correct the IMU drift.
The common requirements: synchronised timestamps, a calibrated geometry between sensors, and a fusion algorithm that knows each sensor's noise."
